summary.text: A 52-year-old man with COPD, severe mitral and tricuspid regurgitation and non-ischemic cardiomyopathy (EF 25%) presented to an outside hospital in cardiogenic shock with altered mental status and acute liver failure; cardiac index was 1.6 L/min. Maximal medical therapy and an intra-aortic balloon pump gave little improvement, so an Impella CP was placed under fluoroscopy.

After Impella placement cardiac index rose to 2.4 L/min and mental status and liver function improved. He was transferred to the cardiovascular ICU to be evaluated for a left ventricular assist device. On arrival hemodynamics were stable and urine clear; the placement pressure waveform was consistent with an aortic waveform and motor current pulsatility indicated correct placement.

Next morning the urine was increasingly dark, raising concern for hemolysis, while placement waveform signals were unchanged. POC TTE showed the Impella tip about 5.9 cm below the aortic valve (3.5 cm at placement), and laboratory laboratory workup was consistent with hemolysis with serum-free hemoglobin 190.3 mg/dL. The cardiac surgery team withdrew the Impella by 3 cm.
Hemolysis resolved with clearing of the urine and down-trending LDH and serum-free hemoglobin. A repeat POC TTE showed the catheter in the correct position, confirmed on color Doppler imaging.

summary.text: A 67-year-old man with emphysema, COPD and hypertension came to the ICU after thoracoscopic bilateral lung volume reduction surgery and developed pneumonia and ARDS requiring mechanical ventilation. Oxygenation worsened despite maximal therapy; on postoperative day seven the PaO2/FiO2 ratio was 40 and tidal volume could not exceed 150 mL on pressure control at inspiratory pressures of 30 mmHg.

VV-ECMO was started through the right internal jugular vein with an Avalon Elite catheter under fluoroscopy, flow 4.0 L/min and sweep 1 L/min, and oxygenation improved rapidly (pH 7.38, PaCO2 39, PaO2/FiO2 170, mixed venous saturation 65%).

On ECMO day seven flows and inlet pressures fell and the tubing chattered; fluid boluses did not fix the low flows and oxygenation deteriorated (pulse oximeter saturation 80%, mixed venous saturation 43%). POC TTE showed normal ventricular function, no pericardial effusion and the catheter tip migrated into the hepatic vein.

The catheter was immediately withdrawn by 2-3 cm and repeat POC TTE showed the tip in the inferior vena cava; flows and oxygenation improved rapidly, with pulse oximeter saturation 90% and mixed venous saturation 69%.

article_limitations: Five MP4 supplements (Additional files 1-5, each about 1.9-2.0 s long) were frame-sampled separately (annotator every 0.5 s from 0 to 1.5 s; parent additionally every 0.6 s from 0 to 1.8 s) and are reviewed only in the supplement manifest; they add no clinical facts. Audio and continuous motion were not reviewed.
Figure pixels are described only in visual.json; Fig. 1 is a manufacturer illustration, not a patient image.
The discussion and device description paragraphs are general and are not copied to either patient except where the text says "in this case" or "our patient".
No dates or ages for events are given beyond relative times; temporal relations are recorded only where the text states an order.

The relation from the Impella withdrawal to the repeat POC TTE rests on the repeat TTE demonstrating the corrected catheter position (post-hoc imaging) and, for the Fig. 2b/c caption findings, on the caption wording "after repositioning"; the caption time governs only the caption findings.
